_comment: INTAKE TEMPLATE — the machine-readable shape scripts/onboard-company.ts consumes.
!! A FILLED COPY OF THIS FILE CONTAINS LIVE PORTAL PASSWORDS. NEVER COMMIT ONE. !!
Copy it OUTSIDE the repo before you type a real secret into it:
cp docs/onboarding/intake-template.json ~/intake/<company>.json
.gitignore is the net under that rule, not a substitute for it: it covers intake/ at any
depth, any filename containing 'intake', every .json at the repo ROOT, and every .json
under docs/ — with this one template negated back in so it stays tracked. Verify rather
than trust, with `git check-ignore -v <your file>`; silence means nothing caught it. A copy
saved elsewhere (backend/cascade-ridge.json) is still committed by the next `git add -A`.
Out of the repo is the rule.
After the run, delete the filled copy: the secrets now live encrypted in
portal_credentials.encrypted_secret, and that file is a second, plaintext copy of them
with no encryption and no access control.
Every value below is FAKE. Replace all of them. Do not ship a run with any string
still reading EXAMPLE, 000000, .invalid, or REPLACE-ME.
Field-by-field WHY / WHAT BREAKS: docs/onboarding/INTAKE_CHECKLIST.md
── THIS SHAPE IS THE SERVICE-BUREAU LANE, WHICH IS THE WHOLE PRODUCT TODAY ──
There is deliberately NO `org` block, NO entitlements key, and an EMPTY `users` list here.
With those three absent, the company lands as a `clients` row inside the operator's
existing tenant (org-default), and that is the COMPLETE path to a staged filing: no org,
no login, no entitlement work. Fill this file in as it ships and it runs; the empty
`users` array is not an omission to complete, it is the correct answer (see point 1).
An `org` block is added ONLY for the own-tenant escalation case — the company signs in as
its own tenant — and that case is a DOCUMENTED DEAD END today, so do not reach for it
casually. POST /api/orgs/:id/users hardcodes role 'operator'; there is no set-password
route, no password-reset route and no role-elevation route, so a brand-new tenant org can
never get its own admin without raw SQL. And an org holding only permit_reviewer /
form_filler can never stage anything at all: 'autopilot' is the wildcard product and is
deliberately apiKeyAuth:false.
If you escalate anyway, NOTHING creates an org without an explicit opt-in: the shape is
org: { createTenant: true, name: '...', edition: 'full', products: ['autopilot'] }, and a
top-level entitlements: ['autopilot'] is an accepted alias for that products key (naming
both, differently, is refused rather than guessed). Without createTenant: true an `org`
block is IGNORED with a loud warning and the client lands in org-default — which is the
safe outcome, and the reason this template ships no org block at all. `users` is REQUIRED
in that lane and only that lane: a tenant with no login is a row nobody can ever reach.
── notes IS PLAINTEXT AND LLM-VISIBLE ──
portalCredentials[].notes reaches a prompt (knowledgeResearchHint feeds it to the research
prompt). Operational hints only. Never a password, never a security answer, never an
account number, never a meter number — those belong in securityAnswers, which rides inside
the encrypted envelope, or nowhere. The script ENFORCES it: a notes value matching
/pass|pwd|answer|ssn|account num|meter/i is a hard validation failure and exits 1. That is
why the notes values below are worded around those words instead of quoting this warning:
the warning lives HERE, in _comment, which the script never scans.
── Three more things worth knowing before you fill it in ──
1. `users` IS EMPTY ON PURPOSE — do not add an entry to onboard a customer. In this lane
the target org IS org-default, so a users entry does not create a login for the solar
company: it creates one inside the OPERATOR'S own tenant, reaching every client the
operator serves. onboard-company.ts REFUSES that (exit 1, nothing written) unless you
pass --allow-operator-org-user, which you want only for your OWN staff. And what you
would get is a trap in both directions: users[].role is ignored (every user created
anywhere lands as `operator`, and updateUser — the only role writer — needs a signed-in
admin actor), while a users[].password IS honoured (the script calls auth.setUserPassword
and writes a real hash). So it is not "cannot log in": it is a login that works forever
as an operator, with no route to change the role and no route to reset the password.
Promotion is raw SQL, by us, deliberately.
2. portalCredentials[].securityAnswers reaches the encrypted envelope ONLY on the
script path. The REST schema (validation.ts portalCredentialCreateSchema) does not
declare the key, so zod strips it silently over HTTP — no error, no answers stored.
3. portalUrl is the load-bearing field, not portalType. Credential lookup matches on
host AND first path segment, so `.../oregon/` vs `.../sandiego/` is the difference
between finding the login and refusing to use it. Store the real entry URL.
── One key is absent on purpose, and one is here but consumed by nothing ──
- client.portalIdentities is OMITTED. updateClient treats that key as a FULL REPLACE, so
a re-run carrying an empty list silently deletes every identity row the client already
had. Add the key only when you are deliberately writing the complete list, e.g.
'portalIdentities': [ { 'portalType': 'OR · Accela Citizen Access',
'installerCompanyLabel': 'EXAMPLE SOLAR LLC', 'installerContactCode': '',
'notes': '' } ]  (with real JSON double quotes).
- jurisdictions IS below, but onboard-company.ts never reads it. It is OPERATOR
REFERENCE DATA, kept here so the answer travels with the intake. To use it, transcribe
it by hand into scripts/onboarding-readiness.ts --jurisdictions
"STATE|AHJ|UTILITY, STATE|AHJ|UTILITY" — that is what tells you which of their
jurisdictions we have actually driven, before you promise anything.
── THE ONBOARDING GUIDE'S PACKET HAS COLUMNS, AND THE SCRIPT WRITES ALL EIGHT ──
Eight answers the customer-facing onboarding guide asks for live in columns as of
migration v18: updatesInbox, billingContactEmail, licenseState, insuranceExpiry and
bondExpiry on the client, and mfaRequired, mfaCodeDestination and feeResponsibility on
each portal credential. Collect all eight on the call — that is the point of the packet.
The dry run prints a `fees` and an `mfa` line for every portal: check them before the
real run. feeResponsibility must be one of card-on-file / customer-pays / mailed-check /
keelix-pays, or "" for not yet agreed (anything else is refused). mfaRequired must be a
JSON true/false. On a RE-RUN, leaving one of these keys out keeps the stored answer; it
does not reset it. An unknown key inside a portalCredentials[] entry (a typo) is named in
the WARNINGS and dropped, same as an unknown client key. The REST API accepts the three
credential answers too; it still does not accept securityAnswers (use this script).

client.notes: EXAMPLE INTAKE — not a real installer. Verify licensing before any real submittal.

portalCredentials.notes: Account holder: Jane Example (office). Operational hints only — this column is stored in the clear and is visible to the model.

portalCredentials.securityAnswers: mother's maiden name: Example; first car: Example
portalCredentials.notes: Account holder: Alex Example (the electrician), not the office. Login emails a one-time code, so every session needs a human.
